question: Under a worst-case k-sparse additive feature model, how many activation dimensions are necessary and sufficient to linearly embed m features while allowing every feature to be recovered by a linear probe to uniform error epsilon?

key_findings.claim: The paper separates linear representation from linear accessibility, two assumptions often bundled together under the LRH.
key_findings.evidence: A feature is an externally specified function z_i:L->R. Linear representation assumes f(l)=A z(l), while linear accessibility requires probe vectors B such that ||B^T f(l)-z(l)||_infinity<epsilon. The capacity question is then reduced from language to recovering all vectors in a chosen support set S after the linear map A.

key_findings.claim: With nonlinear decoding, classical compressed sensing recovers every k-sparse feature vector using O(k log(m/k)) dimensions.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 1 invokes a measurement matrix A and basis-pursuit decoding g(x)=argmin ||z'||_1 subject to x=Az, obtaining exact recovery of all k-sparse z. This is a representation-capacity baseline whose decoder is an optimization algorithm, not a single neural linear probe.

key_findings.claim: Linear encoding and linear recovery are sufficient in d=O(k^2 log(m)/epsilon^2) dimensions for bounded k-sparse inputs.
key_findings.evidence: The upper-bound construction takes A=B with unit-norm Rademacher columns whose pairwise inner products are below mu=epsilon/k. At most k active coordinates then contribute less than k mu=epsilon interference to any decoded coordinate. Hoeffding plus a union bound gives d=O(log(m)/mu^2)=O(k^2 log(m)/epsilon^2).

key_findings.claim: For fixed epsilon, linear recovery needs nearly quadratic dependence on sparsity: d=Omega_epsilon((k^2/log k) log(m/k)), up to logarithmic factors.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 3 states the lower bound for epsilon>k^(3/2)*sqrt(5/m). The proof normalizes the near-unit diagonal of C=B^T A, applies Alon's rank bound to all large principal submatrices, constructs a graph of cross-interference entries above epsilon/k, and uses Turan's theorem plus pigeonhole to find k same-sign interferers that violate the uniform L-infinity error requirement.

key_findings.claim: Successful linear accessibility constrains the cross-geometry B^T A, not representation geometry A^T A or probe geometry B^T B separately.
key_findings.evidence: Only inner products <b_i,a_j> enter the recovered coordinate. Proposition 9 constructs valid A,B for which each feature's representation and probe directions are almost orthogonal, while representation directions are mutually almost parallel and probe directions are mutually almost parallel. Thus neither set alone is identifiable as the unique 'true feature directions' from the LRH requirements.

key_findings.claim: Near-unit norm constraints recover the intuitive geometry of aligned encoder/decoder directions and approximately orthogonal different features.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 11 assumes ||a_i||,||b_i||<=gamma and uniform epsilon recovery. It bounds same-feature normalized alignment below by (1-epsilon)/gamma^2 and bounds cross-feature normalized inner products above by an expression that tends to zero as epsilon->0 and gamma->1. These norm bounds are extra assumptions, not consequences of the LRH alone.

key_findings.claim: The paper states that adding a bias and monotone activation after a linear probe does not evade the asymptotic lower bound for exact binary-feature classification.
key_findings.evidence: For k-sparse Boolean z, Theorem 12 states d=Omega((k^2/log k)log(m/k)) when each feature's presence is linearly separable and k<sqrt(m). Corollary 13 observes that a componentwise monotone activation preserving positive-versus-negative decisions implies an underlying linear threshold, so the same claimed bound applies to ReLU-style probes; the following audit finding identifies a gap in the printed proof.

anchors.section: 5 Activation functions and binary classification / Theorem 12

key_findings.claim: The printed argument does not establish the binary-classification extension as written because it loses the sign of the interfering entries.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 12's proof says it suffices to find 2k entries with |<b_i,a_j>|>1/k. This only guarantees k entries of one common sign, but Equation 76 silently treats the selected entries as positive and concludes (B^T A z)_i>k(1/k). If the common sign is negative, the displayed negative example does not cross the threshold, and adding e_i would exceed the k-sparse budget when all k interferers are used. Page 16 also calls Theorem 2's nearly matching upper bound Omega(k^2 log m), although Theorem 2 and Equation 27 give an O(k^2 log m) upper bound. Corollary 13 depends on Theorem 12, so the activation-function extension requires a repaired proof.

anchors.section: 5 Activation functions and binary classification / Theorem 12

key_findings.claim: The headline conclusion that a layer can store exponentially many features is a worst-case coding existence result, not evidence that an LLM has learned such a code.
key_findings.evidence: The analysis assumes every possible k-sparse z in [-1,1]^m must be uniformly recoverable from an exact additive representation Az. No language model, natural-language feature set, learned activation matrix, SAE, or intervention is evaluated. The discussion also notes that a next layer has only as many actual probes as neurons, so representability of all coordinate probes does not show that the network uses them all.

key_findings.claim: The theory does not identify a canonical feature set or test the causal reality of externally specified feature functions.
key_findings.evidence: Features are defined as arbitrary functions of text independent of a model, and all results begin after choosing z and assuming f=Az. Equivalent or redundant feature vocabularies can change m and k, while correlated language support can be much smaller than the full worst-case k-sparse cube. The paper provides no intervention establishing that individual coordinates z_i are separately used by downstream computation.

method.core_idea: Formalize LRH capacity as a matrix-factorization/recovery problem: A linearly embeds an externally defined m-dimensional feature vector into d activations and B supplies one linear probe per feature, with uniform coordinate error over all bounded k-sparse vectors.
method.mechanism: The upper bound constructs an incoherent Rademacher dictionary so cross-feature interference sums to at most epsilon. The lower bound treats C=B^T A as a low-rank near-identity matrix, forces many large off-diagonal entries through Alon's rank theorem on principal submatrices, and aggregates them into a violating sparse vector using a Turan-graph argument.
assumptions: A fixed, model-independent feature vector z(l) exists and activations equal the exact additive linear code A z(l).
Every z in the full bounded k-sparse cube [-1,1]^m, not merely the support of natural language, must be decoded with uniform L-infinity error.
Each individual feature is in principle accessible by its own linear probe; the existence of m probes is analyzed even though an actual next layer may instantiate far fewer.
Feature sparsity k and amplitude bound are exogenous and do not vary with context, layer, or feature correlations.
No noise, approximation error in f=Az, distributional error criterion, training dynamics, finite data, or learned optimization is modeled.
The geometry uses ordinary Euclidean dot products unless optional norm assumptions are added.
Binary activation-function results require a monotone componentwise activation and exact separation on all k-sparse Boolean inputs.

techniques.role: Separates additive linear encoding A from coordinate-wise linear accessibility B.
Provides the constructive upper bound by controlling every cross inner product.
Uses low rank of B^T A to force large off-diagonal interference.
Applies the rank obstruction locally so the proof obtains many, not merely one, interfering pairs.
Converts absence of low-interference subsets into a dense graph and a row with many interferers.
Constructs valid codes showing A- and B-directions need not separately have intuitive geometry.
Shows extra norm bounds restore same-feature alignment and cross-feature orthogonality.

evaluations.setting: All k-sparse z in R^m under exact additive encoding and arbitrary nonlinear decoding.
evaluations.metric: Embedding dimension d for exact recovery.
evaluations.result: Classical compressed sensing achieves d=O(k log(m/k)) via L1 basis pursuit.
evaluations.baseline: Nonlinear recovery baseline for the paper's linear-decoder problem.

evaluations.setting: All k-sparse z in [-1,1]^m with linear encoder A and linear decoder B.
evaluations.metric: Smallest d guaranteeing uniform coordinate error below epsilon.
evaluations.result: A Rademacher construction gives d=O(k^2 log(m)/epsilon^2).
evaluations.baseline: Classical compressed sensing's linear-in-k dimension, which is unavailable under one-step linear decoding.

evaluations.setting: Same worst-case linear-recovery problem with epsilon>k^(3/2)*sqrt(5/m).
evaluations.result: d=Omega_epsilon((k^2/log k)log(m/k)); the upper and lower bounds differ by logarithmic factors for fixed epsilon.
evaluations.baseline: The constructive O_epsilon(k^2 log m) upper bound.

evaluations.setting: k-sparse Boolean feature vectors with exact per-feature classification; k<sqrt(m).
evaluations.metric: Dimensions needed for linear thresholds or monotone-activation probes.
evaluations.result: Theorem 12 and Corollary 13 claim d=Omega((k^2/log k)log(m/k)) and no asymptotic gain from a bias plus componentwise monotone activation.
evaluations.baseline: Pure linear threshold decoding; the printed proof has an unresolved sign step, so this claimed extension is not treated as established by the reviewed version.

limitations: Author-stated: the paper analyzes a single layer; how multiple layers use, combine, and transform many accessible features remains open.
Author-stated: nonlinear representations with linear accessibility and richer decoders such as two-layer networks are not characterized.
Author-stated: alternative representation hypotheses, including multi-dimensional and nonlinear features, may have different capacities.
Reviewer-identified: there is no LLM experiment, learned-code experiment, SAE measurement, or intervention; the title's language-model claim is an interpretation of an abstract coding theorem.
Reviewer-identified: m is not identifiable without a privileged feature ontology. Duplicating, merging, or reparameterizing feature functions changes the nominal capacity question.

Reviewer-identified: the worst-case full k-sparse cube ignores feature correlations and forbidden co-occurrences, so it can be substantially stricter than language support and does not model constructive interference.
Reviewer-identified: uniform L-infinity recovery and exact Az encoding omit finite-data generalization, probe estimation, activation noise, approximate representation, and average-case error.
Reviewer-identified: existence of m probes does not mean a model stores or uses m causally distinct features, especially when the next layer instantiates only d_next linear functionals.

Reviewer-identified: the proof of Theorem 12 obtains large absolute off-diagonal entries but Equation 76 assumes positive entries; the negative-sign case is not handled within the k-sparse budget, so the Boolean and monotone-activation extension has a proof gap.
failure_modes: Dense feature activation or k growing too quickly with m erodes the exponential-storage interpretation because d scales quadratically in k.
Correlated, mutually exclusive, hierarchical, or redundant features make the full k-sparse support assumption inaccurate and m noncanonical.
Nonlinear or multi-dimensional model features need not admit f=Az and therefore fall outside both bounds.
If encoding is approximate or noisy, small cross terms and recovery error can compound differently from the noiseless proof.
A learned network may not discover the random incoherent construction even though it exists.
Large encoder/decoder norms permit highly unintuitive and potentially unstable geometry; intuitive alignment follows only after additional norm control.
A non-monotone decoder, multi-layer decoder, attention, or contextual routing can exceed the modeled one-probe accessibility class.
Linear probe success can reflect correlation rather than causal use, so capacity estimates based only on accessibility can overcount functional features.
The Boolean-classification and monotone-activation lower bounds should not be reused without repairing the sign case in Theorem 12's interference argument.
reusable_insights: State linear representation and linear accessibility as separate hypotheses; probe success is not equivalent to an additive representation model.
Analyze encoder-decoder cross-geometry B^T A instead of treating SAE encoder or decoder columns alone as the unique feature directions.
Report feature capacity jointly as a function of sparsity, error tolerance, support family, and decoder class; 'features per neuron' is not a scalar invariant.
Use constrained norms or conditioning metrics when geometric interpretability matters, because recovery alone permits nearly parallel dictionaries.
Distinguish representability from computation: being able to decode a coordinate does not show downstream layers actually instantiate or use that decoder.
For empirical tests, compare worst-case combinatorial support bounds with distribution-aware bounds that incorporate real co-activation structure.
open_questions: What are tight dimension bounds for realistic correlated or structured feature supports rather than the full k-sparse cube?
Can SGD in a transformer learn the incoherent codes used in the existence proof, and under what objectives or regularizers?
How do approximate linear representation error and activation noise modify the upper and lower bounds?
What capacity is possible with a two-layer, attention-based, or context-gated decoder?
Can causal interventions distinguish linearly probeable correlates from features actually used by later layers?
Is there a feature-ontology-invariant capacity notion robust to splitting, merging, and invertible reparameterization?
How should capacity be defined for irreducible multi-dimensional, manifold, or magnitude-coded features?
How do layer composition and a finite number of actual downstream neurons convert latent accessibility into computation?
Can Theorem 12's graph argument be strengthened to force k positive interferers, or can a separate construction handle the all-negative case without exceeding k-sparsity?

competitive_landscape.title: Toy Models of Superposition
competitive_landscape.difference: Elhage et al. empirically optimize a tied nonlinear toy autoencoder and observe sparsity-driven polytope phases; Garg et al. abstract away training and nonlinear reconstruction to prove worst-case dimension bounds for arbitrary A,B with linear coordinate recovery.

competitive_landscape.title: The Linear Representation Hypothesis and the Geometry of Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Park et al. derive probing and steering concepts from counterfactual semantics and validate them in LLaMA-2 with a causal inner product; Garg et al. use externally specified feature functions and Euclidean matrix recovery to study capacity, without semantic or causal validation.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Complexity of Neural Computation in Superposition
competitive_landscape.difference: Adler and Shavit bound the neurons and parameters required to compute permutations and logical operations on superposed features and find only polynomial computational capacity; Garg et al. bound one-layer storage with coordinate probes, explicitly leaving downstream computation unresolved.

competitive_landscape.title: From superposition to sparse codes: interpretable representations in neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Klindt et al. use identifiability and sparse coding to argue that nonlinear classifiers recover latent factors up to linear mixing and can be post-hoc disentangled; Garg et al. assume the latent feature vector is already fixed and quantify the extra cost of requiring the decoder itself to be linear.

competitive_landscape.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
competitive_landscape.difference: Engels et al. discover multi-dimensional circular features and causally intervene on them in real LLM tasks; Garg et al.'s m coordinates are scalar additive features, so its storage bounds do not cover an irreducible circle as the computational unit.

competitive_landscape.title: Recurrent Neural Networks Learn to Store and Generate Sequences using Non-Linear Representations
competitive_landscape.difference: Csordas et al. show small gated RNNs use magnitude-based layered codes that cannot be localized in distinct linear subspaces; Garg et al. provide no bound for such nonlinear encodings and explicitly assumes exact additive directions.

competitive_landscape.title: Projecting Assumptions: The Duality Between Sparse Autoencoders and Concept Geometry
competitive_landscape.difference: Hindupur et al. demonstrate that concept dimensionality and nonlinear separability make SAE recovery architecture-dependent; Garg et al.'s capacity m presumes a fixed scalar feature ontology and does not propagate extractor-dependent uncertainty.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv v2 / NeurIPS 2025 Poster; submitted=2025-03-03; revised/source_date=2025-12-01

competitive_landscape.title: Polysemanticity and Capacity in Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Scherlis et al. study which unequal-importance features receive fractional dimension in optimized toy networks and how architecture shapes blocks; Garg et al. assume symmetric worst-case recoverability of every coordinate and derive combinatorial storage bounds rather than learned allocation.

competitive_landscape.title: From Data Statistics to Feature Geometry: How Correlations Shape Superposition
competitive_landscape.difference: Prieto et al. show real co-activation correlations can make interference constructive and shape learned geometry; Garg et al. protects against every bounded k-sparse sign pattern, deliberately excluding distribution-specific cancellation or support restrictions that could lower dimension.

competitive_landscape.title: Spectral Superposition: A Theory of Feature Geometry
competitive_landscape.difference: Ivanov et al. derive eigenspace localization and tight-frame geometry from saturation in a tied toy model; Garg et al. show recovery does not constrain A- or B-geometry without norm assumptions and bounds capacity without assuming tied weights or spectral localization.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper gives nearly matching upper and lower bounds for linear compressed sensing and thereby establishes how many features a language-model layer can store under linear representation plus linear accessibility.
novelty_assessment.evidence: It proves an O(k^2 log m/epsilon^2) incoherent-code upper bound, an Omega_epsilon((k^2/log k)log(m/k)) lower bound, geometry counterexamples, norm-controlled geometry results, and a binary monotone-decoder extension.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The separation of representation from accessibility and the main real-valued lower-bound proof are substantive theoretical contributions. The LLM interpretation is conditional and should not be read as an empirical feature count: the result is for a fixed external ontology, exact additive codes, worst-case sparse support, and one-step coordinate recovery, with no identifiability, training, causal-use, or toy-to-LLM validation. The printed sign gap means the Boolean-classification and monotone-activation extension should be treated as a claim pending proof repair.

reviewer_notes: All 20 extracted pages were independently inspected, including complete proofs and references; PDF pages 5, 16, and 17 were checked directly for theorem notation and the Boolean-extension proof. The upper bound is recorded with its explicit epsilon^{-2} dependence from Equation 27 rather than only O_epsilon notation. The classical compressed-sensing domain was corrected to all k-sparse z in R^m. The audit treats 'exponential storage' as a coding existence claim, not a measured LLM property, and flags the unresolved sign case in Theorem 12. The reviewed paper's current record is arXiv v1 dated 2026-02-11. Ten competitor records were rechecked directly on official arXiv primary records on 2026-08-23, with exact current version URLs and source dates recorded. This is a primary full-text audit, not independent proof verification or replication.
